text: Johnny David Damon, born on November 5, 1973, is an American former professional baseball outfielder who played in Major League Baseball (MLB) from 1995 to 2012. He played for the Kansas City Royals (1995–2000), Oakland Athletics (2001), Boston Red Sox (2002–2005), New York Yankees (2006–2009), Detroit Tigers (2010), Tampa Bay Rays (2011), and Cleveland Indians (2012). He also represented the Thailand national baseball team and was part of the squad for the 2013 World Baseball Classic qualifiers. Damon was born in Fort Riley, a U.S. Army post in Kansas, and his mother, Yome, is a Thai immigrant, while his father, Jimmy, is of Croatian and Irish descent. They met when Jimmy, a staff sergeant in the U.S. Army, was stationed in Thailand, and Damon spent much of his early life as an "Army brat," moving to posts in Okinawa, Japan, and West Germany before settling in the Orlando, Florida, area as a pre-schooler. As a child, Damon was quiet due to a stutter, saying his thoughts raced ahead of his tongue, and he improved through singing; he played in South Orange Little League and for the Walker Jr. High baseball team before attending Dr. Phillips High School in Orlando, where in his senior year (1992) he was rated the top high school prospect by Baseball America, named to USA Today's High School All-America team, and awarded the Florida Gatorade Player of the Year. He also ran track, finishing second in the 200m dash as a senior, and played football, once being hit by Warren Sapp and suffering his first concussion. Selected by the Kansas City Royals in the first round (35th overall) of the 1992 MLB draft, Damon made his MLB debut on August 12, 1995, after playing with the minor league Wichita Wranglers. He played for the Royals from 1995 to 2000, scoring 104 runs in 1998 and 101 in 1999, and in 2000 led the American League in runs (136) and stolen bases (46), finishing second in hits (214), at bats (655), and plate appearances (741). In 2001, he joined the Oakland Athletics in a three-way trade involving the A's, Royals, and Tampa Bay Devil Rays, receiving pitcher Cory Lidle from the Devil Rays and second baseman Mark Ellis from the Royals; he finished third in at bats (644) and seventh in runs (108). On December 21, 2001, he signed a four-year, $31 million contract with the Boston Red Sox. In 2002, he led the league in triples (11) and was third in infield hits (25), becoming the first player selected by fans in the inaugural American League All-Star Final Vote. On June 27, 2003, he became only the second player since 1900 to record three base hits in an inning, against the Florida Marlins; during Game 5 of the 2003 ALDS, he collided head-on with teammate Damian Jackson, suffering a severe concussion and being removed on a stretcher, while Jackson also sustained a concussion but walked off with assistance. In 2004, he was second in runs (123), batted .304 with 20 home runs and 94 RBIs, and was only the fourth leadoff batter in MLB history to drive in over 90 runs in a season; he went 7-for-15 in the Division Series against the Angels but struggled in the ALCS against the Yankees, going 3-for-29 in the first six games, and hit two home runs— including a grand slam—in Game 7 to lead the Red Sox to the pennant, and hit a home run in the World Series as they swept the St. Louis Cardinals, ending the 86-year "Curse of the Bambino" drought. Over his four years with the Red Sox (2002–2005), he appeared in 597 games (590 in center field and seven as a designated hitter), hit 56 home runs, had 2,259 at-bats as a leadoff hitter, and batted second in the lineup for 156 at-bats in 2002, starting two games as the third hitter in 2004, and had 624 at-bats as a leadoff hitter in 2005; he earned his second All-Star selection as the American League center fielder, led the AL in infield hits (35), and matched his 2004 total of 35 doubles. On December 20, 2005, he signed a four-year, $52 million contract with the New York Yankees; the Red Sox declined a five-year deal proposed by agent Scott Boras. His signing led to backlash from many Red Sox fans due to his prior loyalty to the team, including a statement in May 2005 where he said, "There's no way I can go play for the Yankees, but I know they're going to come after me hard. It's definitely not the most important thing to go out there for the top dollar, which the Yankees are going to offer me. It's not what I need." The Yankees had a strict dress code forbidding long hair and facial hair beyond neat mustaches (relaxed in 2025), so Damon had his shoulder-length "cave man" hair cut and beard shaved on December 22; he had planned to do so regardless of signing with the Yankees to avoid speculation. In 2006, he finished third in runs (115) and ninth in stolen bases (25), hitting 24 home runs—his career high—and tied his 35 doubles mark; he was one of only four players in the majors to hit at least 24 home runs and steal at least 24 bases. On June 7, 2008, he went 6-for-6 in a Yankees win over the Kansas City Royals, including a walk-off ground-rule double, becoming the first Yankee to have six hits in a nine-inning game since Myril Hoag in 1934; he said it was his first walk-off as a Yankee. The Yankees placed him on the 15-day disabled list on July 6, 2008, with a bruised AC joint in his left shoulder after colliding with the outfield wall while trying to catch a triple; at the time, he was one of only three active major league players with at least 10 years of experience without being on the disabled list; he returned and hit 27 doubles that season, and hit 53 home runs in his three complete seasons with the Yankees. On July 27, 2009, he hit his 200th career home run against Brian Shouse of the Tampa Bay Rays; he batted .282 and tied for the lead among AL left fielders in errors (5), and was fourth in the league in runs scored (107). He hit home runs in Games 3 and 4 of the 2009 ALCS, defeating the Angels in six games, and stole two bases in one play during the 2009 World Series against the Phillies when the defense was shifted against Mark Teixeira; he earned his second championship ring as the Yankees defeated the Phillies in six games. After winning his second World Series, Damon entered free agency in 2009 despite wanting to return to the Yankees; he insisted the Yankees not offer him a contract unless they paid at least $13 million for the prior four years; as a result, the Yankees signed Nick Johnson to a one-year, $5.5 million deal and Randy Winn to a one-year, $2 million deal, effectively closing the door on his return. On February 20, 2010, he signed a one-year, $8 million deal with the Detroit Tigers; on April 14, he recorded his 1,000th career RBI against the Royals; on May 1, he hit a walk-off home run against Scot Shields of the Angels at Comerica Park to win 3–2; on July 6, he recorded his 2,500th career hit off Jake Arrieta of the Orioles and hit a walk-off home run off David Hernandez, giving the Tigers a 7–5 win; he batted .271 with eight home runs and 51 RBIs that season and became a free agent afterward. On January 21, 2011, he signed a one-year, $5.25 million deal with the Tampa Bay Rays, and the Rays also signed former Red Sox teammate Manny Ramirez in a package deal suggested by agent Scott Boras; Kelly Shoppach, a former Red Sox player, was also reunited with Damon. Manager Joe Maddon expected the 37-year-old to be frequently replaced by Sam Fuld in late-game situations when the Rays were leading; after Ramirez's retirement, Damon primarily played as the designated hitter. On April 16, 2011, he recorded the game-winning hit for the fifth consecutive game for the Rays, two of which were walk-off hits; on June 29, 2011, he tied Ted Williams for 71st on the all-time hit list with 2,654 hits at Tropicana Field in the bottom of the sixth; on July 2, 2011, he went 4-for-4 and his first-inning single moved him past Ted Williams to 72nd on the all-time list, finishing the season 57th with 2,723 career hits. In Game 1 of the ALDS, he hit a two-run home run in the second inning off C. J. Wilson to give the Rays a 2–0 lead, though they eventually lost the best-of-five series 3–1. On April 12, 2012, he signed a one-year minor league contract with the Cleveland Indians for $1.25 million (with an additional $1.4 million in incentives); on May 1, he was called up to Cleveland; he made his debut on May 2, batting leadoff against the Chicago White Sox, finishing 0–3 with a walk; manager Manny Acta dropped him to seventh in the batting order after going 4–29 in the leadoff position, including 2 hits in his last 18 at-bats; on June 26, he became the 52nd player in MLB history to reach 2,750 career hits; heading into the All-Star break, he had 35 hits in 163 official at-bats and was hitting .215 in 50 games; on July 20, he tied a season-high with three hits against the Baltimore Orioles. He was designated for assignment on August 3, 2012, and released by the Indians along with pitchers Derek Lowe and Jeremy Accardo on August 9. Damon finished his career with 2,769 hits, placing him 54th on the MLB all-time career hits list. His first year of eligibility for the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum was in 2018, when he joined a group of first-time candidates including Chipper Jones, Jim Thome, and Omar Vizquel; he received eight votes (1.9% of the ballot) and was dropped from future consideration. Damon hoped to be signed for 2013 and offered the Yankees a contract at the minimum salary to replace injured Curtis Granderson, expressing willingness to be released once Granderson returned; the Yankees indicated no interest, and he remained unsigned throughout 2013 and did not play. In late 2013 and early 2014, he expressed a desire to keep playing to reach 3,000 hits (needing 231), stating he remained in good physical condition and hoped to receive invitations to spring training. He did not receive any offers before the 2014 season; in a May 2014 interview in Boston to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the Red Sox 2004 World Series win, he said he had no plans to officially announce retirement, acknowledged he would likely not play again, but still wanted to play and said, "I feel like if a team calls me, I can be ready. If I play tonight, I'll hit a homer." On June 22, 2014, he played in his first New York Yankees Old-Timers' Day. A July 2014 press report indicated he still hoped to play again in the majors; in June, he completed an impromptu session with a Phillies batting practice pitcher, who suggested the Phillies consider signing him. On August 4, 2014, he stated in an interview with WEEI-FM's "Middays with MFB" that while he wanted to play, no teams had expressed interest and "those days are over." In December 2014, he hoped to play in 2015, and his agent told a reporter, "If you ask Johnny, he'd love to come back." In 2005, Damon authored the book Idiot: Beating "The Curse" and Enjoying the Game of Life with Peter Golenbock. He contributed backing vocals to Dropkick Murphys' 2004 single "Tessie." He hosted WWE Raw on December 21, 2009. He participated in the Celebrity Apprentice competition in spring 2014 in New York City, with the episodes part of the 2015 season; he was eliminated on the episode aired on February 2, 2015. He appeared on the Animal Planet show Tanked in 2016. He appeared on MTV Cribs in 2005, giving a tour of his home near Orlando, Florida.

In 2005, Damon wrote the book *Idiot: Beating "The Curse" and Enjoying the Game of Life* with Peter Golenbock. He contributed backing vocals to Dropkick Murphys' 2004 single "Tessie." Damon hosted WWE Raw on December 21, 2009. In the spring of 2014, he participated in the Celebrity Apprentice competition in New York City, with the shows filmed as part of the 2015 season; he was eliminated on the episode that aired on February 2, 2015. Damon appeared on the Animal Planet show *Tanked* in 2016 and on MTV Cribs in 2005, where he gave a tour of his home near Orlando, Florida. In April 2018, he was announced as one of the celebrities competing on season 26 of *Dancing with the Stars*, partnered with professional dancer Emma Slater; he was eliminated on the first episode and placed ninth. In August 2019, Damon and his wife appeared as primary charter guests during seasons 4 and 5 of *Below Deck Mediterranean*. On February 22, 2023, Damon played in an exhibition game with the Savannah Bananas in a Banana Ball match against the Party Animals at Jackie Robinson Ballpark in Daytona Beach, Florida. Damon has had two marriages and fathered eight children: he married Angela Vannice, his high school sweetheart in 1992, and they divorced in 2002, having twins (a son and a daughter) in 1999; he later married Michelle Mangan in 2004, with whom he has six children—five daughters (including a set of twins) and a son. Damon and his family reside in Windermere, Florida, while with the Yankees, they lived in Cresskill, New Jersey. He is active with the Wounded Warrior Project, which raises awareness and public support for the needs of severely injured service men and women. Damon was one of the victims of the $8 billion fraud committed by convicted wealth manager Allen Stanford. He spoke at a rally in Florida during Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign and chanted in support of a border wall between the United States and Mexico; he formerly served as a committee member on Trump's council on Sports, Fitness, & Nutrition. On October 26, 2019, in Orlando, Florida, Damon was the Special Guest at the Orange County Republican Party's Trump Defender Gala and the 2019 Annual Lincoln Day Dinner. On February 19, 2021, Damon was arrested in Windermere, Florida, for driving while intoxicated (DWI) and for resisting an officer without violence; police reported his blood alcohol content (BAC) was .30, measured two hours after being stopped; bodycam footage released by the Windermere Police Department showed Damon claiming his arrest was part of being targeted due to his support for Trump.
